newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria assures U.S. on military reform.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria assures U.S. on military reform.

text.p: Bulgarian leaders assured U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen on Sunday that the former hard- line Soviet ally was making serious military reforms in its push to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.

"I am satisfied that they are dedicated to military reform ... that they are going to bring their standards up to NATO in the future," Cohen told reporters following security talks with President Petar Stoyanov and Defence Minister Georgi Ananiev.

Cohen, winding up a trip to assure Eastern European democracies that NATO remained open to more new members after inviting Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to join in 1999, said Washington was impressed by recent economic reforms by Sofia's democratic government.

The secretary made no immediate promise of concrete additional U.S. military funds for Bulgaria's Soviet-style armed forces and did not say when Bulgaria, one of the Soviet bloc's most dedicated members during the Cold War, might be ready to join the alliance.

Cohen told reporters that the people of Bulgaria should be proud of Bulgaria's drive toward a free-market economy, a sharp drop in inflation from 500 percent to less than 10 percent and the appointment of Ananiev as the country's first civilian defence minister.
Stoyanov's spokeswoman, Nerry Terzieva, told reporters travelling with Cohen that the president had assured the secretary at lunch that Bulgaria was no longer "emotionally dependent" on Russia.
"There is no nostalgia," she said, adding that Bulgaria was willing to act as a bridge between Moscow and the West after becoming a member of NATO.

Cohen refused to discuss details of the conversation but said "the president indicated that this is a very proud and very independent autonomous country with a rich heritage, willing to work with all parties concerned -- Russia, other European nations and the United States."
"We believe that Bulgaria plays a key role in helping to stabilise the (Balkans) region," Cohen told reporters. The country shares borders with Greece, Turkey, Macedonia, Romania and Serbia.
He cautioned, however, that military cuts must be made carefully.

"It will be important as downsizing takes place that it be reformed in a way that would still maintain an effective capability ... to defend Bulgaria, but also to provide assistance to other NATO countries consistent with Article 5 of the NATO charter," Cohen said.

U.S. defence officials, who asked not to be identified, said they were watching closely to see how Bulgaria's plan to cut its military force from 96,000 troops to about 65,000 within a year will be handled.

The United States currently provides about $6 million in military aid annually to Bulgaria, including funds to support the miltary's active participation in NATO's "Partnership for Peace" defence coopertion programme.
Bulgaria also receives about $35 million annually in U.S. Agency for International Development (AID) help for medical and other civilian projects.

"Your visit here is a real support for the new political majority which has to overcome serious difficulties that come from seven years of political and economic stagnation," civilian Defence Minister Ananiev told Cohen.
Ananiev called the visit "a guarante for the irreversibility of the process of NATO enlargement."
